paras: The Raggio dance hall shooting was a gun battle at a dance at Raggio, twelve miles east of Marianna in Lee County, Arkansas, at about 1 a.m. on Sunday, August 28, 1910, in which two Black men, Mack Harvey and Henry Cox, were killed and three others wounded. It began when a white man, John Russell, returned to the dance with two men the county sheriff called deputy constables to arrest Harvey, and Russell himself was fatally shot. Wire reports of a battle of more than fifty shots between "negroes and whites" ran in papers from Arkansas to Connecticut.

According to a Black man who reached Marianna at daybreak to buy coffins, a dance was in progress when Harvey quarreled with his wife. Russell, a white man, ordered the couple to stop, and Harvey, by this account, "declared he would talk to his wife any way he pleased." Russell left and came back shortly with two other white men, while Harvey, the messenger said, "secured friends and awaited the return of the white men."

The messenger was described as too frightened to give a coherent story of the shooting that followed. Sheriff Ford, after returning from the scene, said the men Russell had brought were deputy constables and that the shooting was "precipitated when Harvey refused to be placed under arrest." More than fifty shots were exchanged.

Harvey and Henry Cox were killed, and Eli Davis, Pleas Bailey and Dault Marchbanks, all Black, were wounded. Russell was first reported "said to be dying," and the Forrest City Times later reported that he had been "shot and killed."

Sheriff Ford arrested half a dozen Black men, four of whom were wounded, one of them probably fatally. The Marianna dispatch reported that excitement ran high but that no immediate outbreak was expected. No report of an inquest, of charges against the arrested men, or of any proceeding over the deaths of Harvey and Cox appears in the coverage.

Nearly all coverage came from one Marianna dispatch dated August 28, which the Montgomery Advertiser printed in full on August 29 under the headline "Dance Ends in Quarrel." The Atlanta Semi-Weekly Journal headed it "Whites and Negroes Battle at Marianna, Ark.," and the Bamberg Herald in South Carolina ran it as "Blood Flows After Dance." The Washington Evening Star cut the story to a paragraph titled "Peacemaker Loses Life," which dropped the messenger's uncertainty and stated that "Harvey started shooting." The Norwich Bulletin reduced it to a single line among its condensed telegrams.

In Arkansas, a shorter boilerplate version, "Two Dead in Dance Hall Row" or "Two Negroes Slain in Dance Hall," ran in the Malvern Times-Journal, the Forrest City Times and the Cotter Courier, naming no Black victims and calling the white man "Ernest Johnson." The Forrest City Times also printed its own local note calling the episode "a general shooting affray at a negro dance" in which Russell had entered "as a peacemaker." Every account rests on the Black messenger's story and the sheriff's report, and none gives the version of Harvey's companions; no coverage in the Black press was found.

The condensed Arkansas version names the white man Ernest Johnson, while the full wire and the local Forrest City note call him John Russell. The Atlanta paper put the Black wounded at four rather than three, a figure that matches the Advertiser's count of wounded men among those arrested. Only the Evening Star says Harvey fired first; the fuller dispatch says the shooting could not be coherently described and gives the sheriff's statement that it began when Harvey refused arrest.

reader.title: Raggio dance hall shooting
bases: Two Black men were killed and others wounded in a gun battle that began, by the sheriff's account, when Mack Harvey resisted arrest by men Sheriff Ford called deputy constables, whom a white man had brought to the dance (A1, A2, A3).

The Marianna wire (A1, A3, A5) and a separate local paragraph in the Forrest City Times (A8) agree that two Black men were killed, three wounded and the white man John Russell shot at a dance near Raggio, although nearly every version traces to one Marianna dispatch built on a Black messenger's story and the sheriff's report (A1).

accounts.label: Black messenger (as relayed by the wire)
accounts.gist: Harvey quarreled with his wife, told Russell he would talk to her as he pleased, and gathered friends while Russell went for two white men; the messenger could not give a coherent account of the shooting itself.

accounts.label: Sheriff Ford
accounts.gist: Russell's two helpers were deputy constables, and the shooting was 'precipitated when Harvey refused to be placed under arrest'.

accounts.label: Evening Star wire condensation
accounts.gist: Russell returned with two officers to arrest Harvey, and 'Harvey started shooting'.

accounts.label: Forrest City Times local note
accounts.gist: Russell, who had entered the dance as a peacemaker, was shot and killed in a general shooting affray.

framing.detail: The Marianna dispatch ran under headlines such as 'Dance Ends in Quarrel', 'Whites and Negroes Battle' and 'Blood Flows After Dance', carrying the sheriff's arrest account without comment.
The Evening Star headed its item 'Peacemaker Loses Life' and said Harvey 'started shooting', casting the white man as a peacemaker and Harvey as the aggressor.
The Forrest City Times called it a 'general shooting affray at a negro dance' and Russell a peacemaker, in a local news column among advertisements.

conflicts.note: Only the condensed boilerplate (A5, reprinted in A7, A9) uses 'Ernest Johnson'; the full wire and the local Forrest City note both say John Russell, which is the better-supported name.

info: About 1 a.m. Sunday, August 28, 1910, at a dance that began Saturday night
A dance hall at Raggio, twelve miles east of Marianna, Arkansas
Killed: Mack Harvey and Henry Cox (Black). Wounded: Eli Davis, Pleas Bailey, Dault Marchbanks (Black). White man John Russell (called 'Ernest Johnson' in a condensed version) fatally shot.
Harvey quarreled with his wife at the dance, refused Russell's order to stop, and, by the sheriff's account, refused to be placed under arrest; no formal charge is named.
John Russell, a white man, and two white men he brought back, whom Sheriff Ford called deputy constables; the Evening Star calls them 'two officers'. Harvey and the friends he gathered fired as well.

sources.note: Fullest Marianna, Aug. 28 wire: names dead Mack Harvey and Henry Cox and three wounded; Russell 'said to be dying'; Sheriff Ford says Russell's helpers were deputy constables; half a dozen arrested, four of them wounded.
quotes: Harvey turned on the white man and declared he would talk to his wife any way he pleased.
He said the men whom Russell secured to aid him were deputy constables and that the shooting was precipitated when Harvey refused to be placed under arrest.
The negro message bearer was too frightened to give a coherent story of the shooting which followed.
High excitement prevails, though no immediate outbreak is anticipated.
